attribution: Dose rates are typical manufacturer ranges; enzyme and fining products vary in activity between suppliers, so bench trials are the only reliable guide. Allergen status is noted where it applies — isinglass, gelatin, chitosan and lysozyme all carry declaration requirements in some markets.

additives.name: Pectic Enzyme
additives.description: Breaks down pectin, the structural polysaccharide that makes fruit musts cloudy, viscous and hard to press.
additives.usageNotes: Add to the crushed fruit before fermentation for both juice yield and clarity; 24 hours of contact before pressing typically lifts yield noticeably.
additives.cautions: Inhibited by high alcohol, so it works far better pre-fermentation than after. Sulphite at normal doses is tolerated.
additives.attribution: 27 CFR 24.246, Materials authorized for the treatment of wine and juice, retrieved from the eCFR versioner API as of 2026-08-01, authorises Pectinase for use in wine and juice. What it regulates is provenance, not dose: the enzyme activity must be derived from Aspergillus niger, and the preparation must be made from nontoxic and nonpathogenic microorganisms. No quantity limit is set for any enzyme in the section. The dose range on this record is therefore unsourced - and it could not come from a statute in any case, because enzymes are dosed on activity units rather than on mass, and two preparations of the same enzyme at the same grams per litre can differ several fold in what they actually do.

additives.name: Alpha-Amylase
additives.description: Cuts starch chains internally to dextrins. Used where the grist has more starch than the malt's own enzymes can convert.
additives.usageNotes: For starch hazes, unmalted-adjunct mashes, and rescuing a mash that failed conversion.
additives.cautions: Does not by itself produce a fully fermentable wort — it makes dextrins, not simple sugars.
additives.attribution: 27 CFR 24.246, Materials authorized for the treatment of wine and juice, retrieved from the eCFR versioner API as of 2026-08-01, authorises Carbohydrase (alpha-Amylase) for use in wine and juice. What it regulates is provenance, not dose: the enzyme activity must be derived from Aspergillus niger, Aspergillus oryzae, Bacillus subtilis, barley malt, or Rhizopus oryzae, and the preparation must be made from nontoxic and nonpathogenic microorganisms. No quantity limit is set for any enzyme in the section. The dose range on this record is therefore unsourced - and it could not come from a statute in any case, because enzymes are dosed on activity units rather than on mass, and two preparations of the same enzyme at the same grams per litre can differ several fold in what they actually do.

additives.name: Glucoamylase
additives.description: Cleaves glucose from the ends of dextrin chains, converting essentially all remaining carbohydrate to fermentable sugar.
additives.usageNotes: The basis of Brut IPA and of most grain-based distilling washes. Also the enzyme in commercial 'light' beers.
additives.cautions: It does not denature at fermentation temperature and will keep working in the bottle — a bottled beer dosed with glucoamylase can ferment to dryness and over-pressurise. Pasteurise or keg.
additives.attribution: 27 CFR 24.246, Materials authorized for the treatment of wine and juice, retrieved from the eCFR versioner API as of 2026-08-01, authorises Carbohydrase (Glucoamylase, Amyloglucosidase) for use in wine and juice. What it regulates is provenance, not dose: the enzyme activity must be derived from Aspergillus niger, Aspergillus oryzae, Rhizopus oryzae or Rhizopus niveus, and the preparation must be made from nontoxic and nonpathogenic microorganisms. No quantity limit is set for any enzyme in the section. The dose range on this record is therefore unsourced - and it could not come from a statute in any case, because enzymes are dosed on activity units rather than on mass, and two preparations of the same enzyme at the same grams per litre can differ several fold in what they actually do.

additives.name: Beta-Glucanase
additives.description: Degrades beta-glucans, the gums from unmalted or under-modified grain that cause set mashes and slow runoff.
additives.usageNotes: Useful with high proportions of raw wheat, rye or oats, and for botrytised musts where the glucan load blocks filtration.
additives.cautions: Works best in the mash; less effective once the wort is hot.
additives.attribution: 27 CFR 24.246, Materials authorized for the treatment of wine and juice, retrieved from the eCFR versioner API as of 2026-08-01, authorises Cellulase (beta-glucanase) for use in wine and juice. What it regulates is provenance, not dose: the enzyme activity must be derived from Trichoderma longibrachiatum or Trichoderma harzianum, and the preparation must be made from nontoxic and nonpathogenic microorganisms. No quantity limit is set for any enzyme in the section. The dose range on this record is therefore unsourced - and it could not come from a statute in any case, because enzymes are dosed on activity units rather than on mass, and two preparations of the same enzyme at the same grams per litre can differ several fold in what they actually do.

additives.name: Lysozyme
additives.description: An egg-white enzyme that lyses gram-positive bacteria — which means lactic acid bacteria, and so malolactic conversion.
additives.usageNotes: Suppresses lactic bacteria without sulphite, useful for delaying or preventing malolactic conversion in a low-sulphite wine.
additives.cautions: An egg-derived allergen requiring declaration in most markets. Does nothing against Brettanomyces or acetic bacteria, which are not gram-positive.

additives.name: Bentonite
additives.description: A negatively-charged clay that binds and drops positively-charged proteins — the standard protection against heat-unstable protein haze in white wine.
additives.usageNotes: Hydrate in water for several hours before use. Bench-trial for the minimum effective dose.
additives.cautions: Strips aroma and colour along with the protein, and makes substantial lees — expect 3-5% volume loss.
additives.attribution: 27 CFR 24.246, Materials authorized for the treatment of wine and juice, retrieved from the eCFR versioner API as of 2026-08-01, authorises Alumino-silicates (hydrated) e.g., Bentonite (Wyoming clay) and Kaolin for treating wine or juice and prints "None" in its limitation column - there is no statutory ceiling on this fining agent, only a requirement that it meet the referenced FDA standard. So the law confirms the material is permitted and says nothing at all about the rate. The dose range on this record is this project's own working guidance and is not sourced; it is cited here because a permitted-materials list with an explicit "None" is a stronger statement than a vendor homepage, not because it establishes the numbers.

additives.name: Isinglass
additives.description: Collagen from fish swim bladders, the traditional cask-ale fining. Drops yeast without stripping much flavour.
additives.usageNotes: The clarity mechanism behind bright cask beer. Works best cold and on already-flocculent yeast.
additives.cautions: Not vegan or vegetarian, and requires allergen declaration in some markets. Degrades if stored warm.
additives.attribution: 27 CFR 24.246, Materials authorized for the treatment of wine and juice, retrieved from the eCFR versioner API as of 2026-08-01, authorises Isinglass for treating wine or juice and prints "None" in its limitation column - there is no statutory ceiling on this fining agent, only a requirement that it meet the referenced FDA standard. So the law confirms the material is permitted and says nothing at all about the rate. The dose range on this record is this project's own working guidance and is not sourced; it is cited here because a permitted-materials list with an explicit "None" is a stronger statement than a vendor homepage, not because it establishes the numbers.

additives.name: Gelatin
additives.description: A positively-charged protein fining that binds tannin and polyphenols, clarifying and softening astringency.
additives.usageNotes: Effective in cold beer and in over-tannic red wine. Dissolve in warm water, never boiling.
additives.cautions: Destroyed by the proteases in fresh pineapple, papaya and kiwi. Over-fining strips colour and body from red wine.
additives.attribution: 27 CFR 24.246, Materials authorized for the treatment of wine and juice, retrieved from the eCFR versioner API as of 2026-08-01, authorises Gelatin (food grade) for treating wine or juice and prints "None" in its limitation column - there is no statutory ceiling on this fining agent, only a requirement that it meet the referenced FDA standard. So the law confirms the material is permitted and says nothing at all about the rate. The dose range on this record is this project's own working guidance and is not sourced; it is cited here because a permitted-materials list with an explicit "None" is a stronger statement than a vendor homepage, not because it establishes the numbers.

additives.name: Sparkolloid
additives.description: A positively-charged polysaccharide fining that works where bentonite alone leaves a persistent pectin or polysaccharide haze.
additives.usageNotes: Boil in water before use. The go-to for stubborn fruit-wine and mead hazes.
additives.cautions: Produces light, fluffy lees that are easily disturbed — rack carefully.
additives.attribution: No citation, because there is no document. Sparkolloid is a proprietary polysaccharide fining agent; it does not appear by name in 27 CFR 24.246, and searching both the 2025-2026 Scott Laboratories Winemaking Handbook and the 2026-2027 Cidermaking Handbook returns nothing for it. The record previously cited the Scott Laboratories homepage. The dose range is this project's own working guidance.

additives.name: Kieselsol & Chitosan
additives.description: A two-part system: negatively-charged silica sol followed by positively-charged chitosan, so each drops what the other leaves behind.
additives.usageNotes: Fast and effective — usually brilliant within 48 hours. The most common homebrew clearing kit.
additives.cautions: Chitosan is usually crustacean-derived and an allergen, though fungal-derived versions exist. Add in the stated order.
additives.attribution: 27 CFR 24.246, Materials authorized for the treatment of wine and juice, retrieved from the eCFR versioner API as of 2026-08-01, authorises Silica gel (colloidal silicon dioxide), and chitosan from Aspergillus niger and sets a numeric ceiling: silica gel "must not exceed the equivalent of 20 pounds colloidal silicon dioxide at a 30 percent concentration per 1000 gallons (2.4 g/L)" and must be completely removed by filtration, while chitosan "must not exceed 0.04 pounds per 1 gallon (500 g/100 L)". The tighter of the two, 2.4 g/L, is the binding one for this pair. The stored maximum of 0.5 g/L sits well inside that, so the statute bounds this record without changing it. The dose range itself is this project's working guidance - the statute gives a maximum, never a recommended rate.

additives.name: PVPP
additives.description: A synthetic polymer that selectively adsorbs polyphenols, removing browning precursors and harsh bitterness.
additives.usageNotes: Used for chill-haze prevention in beer and for pinking and bitterness in white wine.
additives.cautions: Insoluble and filtered out entirely, so nothing remains in the finished drink. Over-use strips desirable phenolics too.
additives.attribution: 27 CFR 24.246, Materials authorized for the treatment of wine and juice, retrieved from the eCFR versioner API as of 2026-08-01, authorises Polyvinylpolypyrrolidone (PVPP) and sets a numeric ceiling: "must not exceed 60 pounds per 1000 gallons (7.19 g/L) and must be removed during filtration". The stored maximum of 0.5 g/L sits well inside that, so the statute bounds this record without changing it. The dose range itself is this project's working guidance - the statute gives a maximum, never a recommended rate.

additives.name: Irish Moss / Whirlfloc
additives.description: A seaweed-derived carrageenan added in the last 10-15 minutes of the boil to coagulate hot-break protein.
additives.usageNotes: One Whirlfloc tablet per 20 L is the standard homebrew dose.
additives.cautions: Does nothing for chill haze — it works on hot break only.
additives.attribution: No citation, because there is no document. Irish moss and Whirlfloc are brewing kettle finings - carrageenan from Chondrus crispus - and 27 CFR 24.246, which governs wine and juice, does not list them; neither Scott Laboratories handbook mentions them either. The record previously cited the Scott Laboratories homepage. The dose range is this project's own working guidance.

additives.name: Activated Carbon
additives.description: Non-selective adsorbent for colour and off-aromas. In distilling, the standard polish for neutral spirit.
additives.usageNotes: Different grades target colour or odour. In spirits, carbon filtration is what turns a rough sugar-wash distillate into vodka.
additives.cautions: Strips everything, good and bad. Bench-trial and use the minimum that works — this is the step where a spirit loses its character.
additives.attribution: 27 CFR 24.246, Materials authorized for the treatment of wine and juice, retrieved from the eCFR versioner API as of 2026-08-01, authorises Activated carbon and sets a numeric ceiling: for removing colour, "the amount used to treat the wine, including the juice from which the wine was produced, must not exceed 25 pounds per 1000 gallons (3 g/L)", and exceeding it requires a notice to TTB under 27 CFR 24.242. The stored maximum of 1 g/L sits well inside that, so the statute bounds this record without changing it. The dose range itself is this project's working guidance - the statute gives a maximum, never a recommended rate.
